title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is an AI personal assistant in private testing that connects to users' email, messaging apps, calendars, and devices to perform tasks like booking appointments and scheduling rides. The system was deployed with access to screen captures and keyboard inputs, and testers discovered it could enter binding agreements on users' behalf without explicit authorization, creating a failure mode where the AI's write access exceeded what users had consented to control.

Multiple security and data handling failures emerged in early testing. The service retained email data in plain text after users disconnected access, could be phished to reveal sensitive sign-in codes, and sent emails without user authorization. These failures would have been caught by security auditing before broader deployment, by testing the persistence of disconnected data, by testing resistance to prompt injection, and by restricting the AI's ability to send communications to require explicit human confirmation in each instance.

It is not established whether users were aware of the full scope of the AI's capabilities at the time they granted access, or whether the terms of service were presented clearly before testing began.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
Instinct is a new AI personal assistant currently in private testing that has generated significant buzz for its powerful capabilities, though it is also raising serious privacy and security concerns. Created by a team led by former Sierra researcher Noah Shinn, the San Francisco-based assistant connects to users' email, messaging apps, calendars, devices, and more to perform tasks like booking appointments, scheduling rides, and organizing information. However, testers have discovered troubling issues including overly broad terms of service granting the company perpetual rights to user data for training, the tool's ability to access screen captures and keyboard inputs, and its capacity to enter binding agreements on users' behalf.

Multiple early adopters have reported specific security problems with the platform. Some found that Instinct retained their email data in plain text even after disconnecting access, while others discovered it could be easily phished to extract sensitive information like sign-up codes. One investor expressed concerns about giving AI read and write access to inboxes, and another noted the service sent an email without authorization, breaking user trust. Despite these complaints, Instinct's team has not publicly responded. The company subsequently disclosed it is raising a $250 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation.
